A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GMM-based graph augmentation work despite the title change and renaming to GRATIN. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original graph-classification, structural-corruption, influence-score, density-estimation ablation, and runtime results.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds filtering experiments, augmentation controls, larger-dataset evaluations, and confidence/entropy analyses.

M1.justification: The original GNN training, class-specific GMM fitting, sampling, and classifier fine-tuning pipeline remains. Section 3.5 adds Fisher-guided filtering: candidates are ranked using validation-set influence scores computed over post-readout parameters, and selected candidates are used for fine-tuning. This is a substantive new selection component.

E1.justification: Appendix L adds COLLAB and REDDIT-MULTI-5K, extending evaluation to datasets containing roughly 5,000 graphs and substantially denser or larger graph structures. The five original datasets and structural-corruption scenarios remain.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark, robustness, and density-estimation comparisons retain their comparator sets. NoisyGNN and the GAN, VBI, KDE, and copula alternatives already appeared in v2. The new controls reuse existing methods under changed settings, while the larger-dataset comparisons extend the existing roster.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs vary the fraction of influence-filtered augmentations and constrain baseline methods to one fixed augmentation per graph across epochs (Tables 8–9). Larger-dataset comparisons introduce a two-hour augmentation cutoff. Existing backbone sizes and training budgets remain; newly specified split details do not establish that earlier experiments changed.

E4.justification: v3 adds a filtering-fraction sensitivity experiment (Figure 3), fixed-augmentation controls (Tables 8–9), and confidence/entropy diagnostics investigating GIN saturation on DD (Appendix M). The configuration-model, density-estimation, and structural-corruption analyses already existed in v2.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies 10-fold cross-validation and explicitly identifies Figure 3 as a single training run. Both versions already report standard deviations. These disclosures do not establish additional runs, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v3 adds filtering, fixed-augmentation, larger-dataset, and confidence-distribution results. Larger-dataset findings are mixed: on COLLAB with GIN, GRATIN reports 79.08% versus SubMix's 80.98% (Table 13). Retained results also receive numerical edits: Table 1's GCN/MUTAG augmentation standard deviation changes from 6.47 to 6.74, and Table 2's unaugmented GIN/MUTAG deviation changes from 11.82 to 2.12. Table 7 fills previously blank SubMix/DD runtime entries.

T1.justification: v3 adds Proposition 3.2 relating embedding perturbations to KL divergence, its Appendix B proof, and GCN/GIN Lipschitz derivations in Appendix D. The augmentation formalism also explicitly accommodates graph-label pairs. The original Rademacher and influence-function bounds remain, with the influence theorem renumbered from 3.3 to 3.4.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims about GMM augmentation, generalization, robustness, efficiency, and Rademacher/influence-function analysis. The added empirical-validation contribution bullet restates performance claims already made in v2; renaming and additional supporting evidence do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v3 proposes a substantive explanation for the existing DD/GIN failure, linking Softmax saturation to unnormalized representations and negligible influence scores. It also discusses augmentation quality versus diversity during filtering and explains hidden-space augmentation's advantages for combining structural and feature information while avoiding node alignment.

D1.justification: Appendix K adds 80%/10%/10% split proportions, degree one-hot encoding for featureless graphs, and feature counts, and updates the reported code pointer to GRATIN. Hardware, backbone dimensions, training schedules, EM stopping criteria, and component counts remain. Detailed EM update equations from v2 are abbreviated to a reference.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning within GNN generalization research, discussing VC-dimension, PAC-Bayesian, and neural-tangent-kernel approaches and distinguishing graph-classification challenges from node-focused work. It adds corresponding references, including Garg, Liao, and Du, alongside Fisher-information and KL-bound literature. Publication-metadata updates are separate from these substantive additions.

P1.justification: Beyond retitling and renaming, v3 rewrites the mathematical formalism and motivation, expands explanatory passages, moves GMM background and experimental setup into appendices, and substantially reorganizes the appendix sequence. Considerable original prose remains, but the narrative structure changes extensively.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column conference layout, and retained tables are reformatted, including replacing colored rankings with bold and underlining. v3 adds Tables 8–9 and 12–13 and Figures 3–8. Original dataset and component-count tables remain as Tables 10–11, with the dataset table expanded.

improvement.justification: v3 improves empirical breadth and documentation through larger-dataset tests, augmentation controls, saturation diagnostics, and fuller setup reporting. However, its new Proposition 3.2 proof invokes ab <= (a-b)^2/2 for positive a and b (Appendix B), which is false at a=b=1, making the added theoretical justification unreliable as written. Fisher filtering is supported only by the single-run PROTEINS curve in Figure 3. These substantive benefits and reliability problems prevent a confident net judgment of overall quality.
